analysis.one_liner: Makes ocean dumpers strictly liable for cleanup costs and damages, with liability caps and resource trustees to restore harm.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee for over a year, got one hearing and one agency comment, and expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a new liability chapter into the 1972 ocean dumping law. Anyone who dumps material at sea — or owns the dumped material or the vessel involved — would be strictly, jointly and severally liable for cleanup costs and for damages to natural resources, property, government revenues, and lost profits [S3]. It would designate federal, state, and tribal trustees to assess the harm and restore the damaged resources, and it would close an 1851 shipping-law loophole that lets vessel owners cap their liability [S2] [S3]. It died in committee without ever reaching the House floor [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, fishing businesses, and property owners who could recover lost profits and property damage from dumpers; taxpayers, because dumpers rather than the public would pay removal costs; and federal, state, and tribal governments, which would gain trustee authority and dedicated funds to assess and restore damaged ocean resources [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes anyone who dumps at sea — plus the dumper's transporters, vessel owners, and owners of the dumped material — jointly, severally, and strictly liable for removal costs and damages, so cleanup does not fall on the public [S3].
Lets anyone whose property or earning capacity is hurt by dumping recover damages, including lost profits, and lets governments recover lost tax and royalty revenues [S3].
Requires federal, state, and Indian tribe trustees to assess injuries to natural resources and implement restoration plans, with recovered money reserved only for those restoration costs [S2] [S3].

Removes the 1851 Limitation of Liability Act shield for ocean dumping and lifts the bill's own liability caps when dumping results from gross negligence, willful misconduct, or violation of a federal regulation [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ocean dumping operators, waste haulers, vessel owners, and companies whose waste is dumped at sea would bear cleanup costs, damage payments, and the insurance costs of covering that liability; some costs would likely be passed on in disposal prices [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Ocean dumpers, haulers, and vessel owners

drawbacks.text: The bill sets dollar caps on liability — the greater of $1,200 per gross ton, $10 million for large vessels, or $2 million for smaller ones — so even after the bill, victims of a catastrophic dump could be left uncompensated above the cap unless gross negligence or a regulatory violation is proven [S3].

Strict joint-and-several liability can pull peripheral parties, such as vessel owners or waste generators with little control over the dumping, into costly litigation; disposal companies would likely pass the added insurance and liability costs on to the municipalities and businesses that pay for waste disposal [S3].

Dumping that is 'permitted or otherwise authorized by Federal, State, or local law' is a complete defense, so the bill imposes no liability at all for the lawful, permitted dumping that makes up most ocean disposal [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would shift the cost of ocean dumping accidents from the public onto the parties that profit from dumping, and give governments real tools to restore damaged resources; the main honest cost is higher waste-disposal prices and the residual risk that the liability caps still leave the public paying above them in the worst cases.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee and two of its subcommittees, got one hearing in February 1992, and never came out of committee before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gerry Studds introduced the bill on November 14, 1991, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Merchant Marine and Fisheries [S5].

On November 21, 1991, it was sent to the Subcommittee on Oceanography, Great Lakes, and the Outer Continental Shelf and the Subcommittee on Fisheries and Wildlife Conservation and the Environment, and executive comment was requested from Commerce, the Army Corps of Engineers, and EPA [S5].
A subcommittee hearing was held on February 20, 1992, and the Justice Department submitted executive comment on July 7, 1992, but the committee never voted the bill out [S5].
The bill drew no cosponsors [S4] and expired with the 102nd Congress on January 3, 1993 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ocean dumping operators, waste haulers, and vessel owners are better off: without the law, they continued to face no new strict liability for cleanup costs or damages, and the old 1851 liability cap remained available to them.

for.name: Rep. Gerry Studds
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and chaired the committee to which it was referred; held a subcommittee hearing on it.

against.name: House Committee on Merchant Marine and Fisheries
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled a markup in the thirteen months before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote and drew no recorded opponents or cosponsors, so the partisan shape of the fight cannot be measured from the record.

industries.industry: Ocean dumping operators and marine waste haulers
industries.note: The bill would have made them strictly liable for cleanup costs and damages from dumping, ending a regime where the public often absorbed those costs. Their gain from the bill's death is the public's continued exposure.
The bill would have made vessel owners liable alongside dumpers and expressly removed the 1851 Limitation of Liability Act cap for dumping damages, raising the cost of marine liability coverage.
These businesses would gain a legal right to recover lost profits and property damage when dumping hurts the resources they depend on.
